narr: Tropical Cyclone Helene began organizing over the western Caribbean on the 23rd and 24th of September before rapidly intensifying as it moved north through the eastern Gulf of Mexico on the 25th and 26th. A plume of moisture extending from the intensifying storm interacted with a slow-moving cold front to produce a band of widespread heavy rain showers and embedded scattered thunderstorms over the southern Appalachians and vicinity on the 25th and 26th, resulting in a predecessor heavy rainfall event over the mountains and portions of the foothills. Helene made landfall in the Florida Big Bend and moved quickly N/NE through Georgia before turning toward the N/NW once the remnant center reached northeast Georgia. Tropical rainbands around the center of Helene swept over areas with already-saturated soils over the mountains and foothills during the early morning of the 27th, resulting in very heavy rainfall and significant flash flooding across multiple basins with headwaters near the Blue Ridge escarpment. Due to its quick movement, Helene was still a strong tropical storm when the wind field reached the western Carolinas and northeast Georgia. Frequent wind gusts of 55 to 70 mph, with occasional gusts of 80 mph...and likely as high as 90 mph across the higher elevations combined with saturated soils to produce widespread damage to trees and electrical infrastructure. Hundreds of trees fell on houses, vehicles, and power lines throughout the area, resulting in several fatalities. Almost all customers in several counties lost power for at least a brief period. Most people were without power for at least a couple of days, while thousands were without power for a week or more.
ev: Stream gauges across the Pacolet River basin indicated flash flooding developed after 10-15 inches of rain fell across northern Spartanburg County over three days, with even heavier rainfall occurring over the headwaters in the mountains. The North Pacolet inundated several roads in the north part of the county, including Highway 14, roads near the water treatment plant. Several tributaries of also overflowed their banks, including Buck Creek, which inundated several secondary roads, and Lawsons Fork Creek in Spartanburg, which overflowed onto Heathwood Dr and Lake Forest Dr, as well as at least one private drive. Additionally, the South Pacolet flooded areas of Depot St and Highway 11 in Campobello, while backwater effects into Motlow Creek caused inundation of Old Mill Rd. Other tributaries flooded throughout the norther part of the county, including a tributary of Dillard Creek, which flooded East Howell Rd in Greer. An 88-year-old male was killed when his vehicle was submerged in floodwater near Landrum.

A stream gauge on the Saluda River in west Greenville indicated flash flooding developed along the river after 8-15 inches of rain fell across the foothills in three days, with 1.5 to 2.5 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. Multiple homes and structures were inundated and damaged on the Pickens County side of the river in east Easley, including on Shop Ct, Shady Acres Circle, Covenant Dr, and Easley Bridge Rd.

Stream gauges and emergency management reported significant flash flooding developed along all major river basins in central Greenville County after 8-15 inches of rain fell across the foothills in three days, with 1.5 to 2.5 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. Flash flooding developed along the Saluda River, with the stream gauge in west Greenville reaching major flood stage, indicating multiple roads and some structures were inundated, including on Riverview Circle. Moderate flooding developed along the Reedy River through the city of Greenville, with extensive flooding of the greenway from Unity Park downstream to Cleveland Park and inundation of multiple roads, including Hudson St, which was damaged and closed for months. Brushy Creek overflowed its banks on the eastside of Greenville and inundated multiple roads, including Edwards Rd, where water entered several homes and Devenger Rd. Significant flooding developed along the Enoree River, with a gauge on the river at Pelham reaching its highest level since August 1995 (Tropical Cyclone Jerry). Inundated roads along the river included Gibbs Shoals Rd.

A stream gauge on the Broad River at Blacksburg (gauge dropped out around 00Z on the 27th) indicated flash flooding developed along the river after extreme rainfall occurred over the headwaters across the mountains and foothills, while rainfall over Cherokee County was generally between 6 and 10 inches over two days. A portion of Little Hope Rd and River Rd was inundated, as were various secondary roads. Access roads to Cherokee Falls and Gaston Shoals dams were also inundated.

A stream gauge on Twelvemile Creek near Liberty indicated flash flooding developed along the stream after 11 to 17 inches of rain fell over three days, with 1 to 2 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. In addition to the creek inundating portions of Concord Church Rd and Riggins Bridge Rd, the grounds of the Pickens County Flea Market were covered with up to 5 feet of water.

Stream gauges indicated flash flooding developed over the headwaters of the Saluda River basin after 15-20 inches of rain, with locally higher amounts fell across the area over three days, with 1.5 to 3 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. The Middle Saluda and smaller tributaries overflowed their banks in the River Falls community, inundating portions of River Falls Rd, Devils Fork Rd, Oil Camp Rd, and Gap Creek Rd, where a house was inundated. Additionally, the North Saluda overflowed onto Old Settlement Rd near Highway 11 and inundated a farm off Bates Bridge Rd.

A stream gauge on the Catawba River indicated flash flooding developed after 5-9 inches of rain fell over the basin over two days. One to two inches of that fell in less than six hours during the morning of the 27th. The main impacts were just downstream of the Highway 21 bridge, where Herrons Ferry Rd and Brakefield Rd and adjacent parks/greenways and parking lots were inundated. Additionally, Wildcat Creek briefly overtopped its banks and inundated McConnells Highway.

Stream gauges indicated flash flooding developed along Durbin Creek near Fountain Inn and along Little River in Laurens after 7-10 inches of rain fell across Laurens County over three days, with 2.5 to 3.5 inches of that falling in less than 3 hours during the morning of the 27th. Durbin Creek inundated Sullivan Rd and Jones Mill Rd. Meanwhile, Little River inundated parks and greenways in Laurens.

Stream gauges on the Saluda River in west Greenville and west Pelzer indicated flash flooding developed along the river after 8-15 inches of rain fell across the foothills in three days, with 1.5 to 2.5 inches of that falling in less than three hours on the morning of the 27th. Multiple homes and structures were inundated and damaged on the Anderson County side of the river from Powdersville down to Pelzer, including on Lakeview Dr, Birch River Rd, and on River Rd. A 60-year-old woman was killed when her vehicle was swept away in floodwater.
